title: The Pretext of Prisons: Tocqueville in America and the Old Regime at Home
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The House the Terror Left Standing

stops.name: Paris, birth into a house the guillotine had emptied
stops.date_confidence: attested (en.wikipedia, fr.wikipedia)
stops.campa: Alexis-Charles-Henri Clérel de Tocqueville is born in Paris on the twenty-ninth of July, into an old Norman family that has recently finished counting its dead. His great-grandfather Malesherbes, who defended Louis XVI before the Convention, went to the guillotine on 22 April 1794 with his daughter, his granddaughter, and her husband. The boy's parents were held for the same reason and released when Thermidor came. He grows up in a house where the Revolution is not a doctrine to be argued about but a bereavement nobody in the room needs explained.
suggested_refs: Portraits of Malesherbes, defender of Louis XVI, executed 22 April 1794
sources: en.wikipedia, Chrétien Guillaume de Lamoignon de Malesherbes

stops.name: Metz, the prefect's son at the Collège Royal
stops.date_confidence: year attested (fr.wikipedia); month of the family's move not established
stops.campa: Hervé de Tocqueville is made prefect of the Moselle and the family goes east to Metz, where Alexis enters the Collège Royal, later the Lycée Fabert. The Moselle is a frontier department and his father administers it for a king brought back by allied armies. Alexis is a prefect's son in a garrison town on the German border, reading his way through his father's library without supervision and without a tutor's list. He takes his baccalauréat here in 1823 and leaves with six years of that library behind him.
suggested_refs: The Lycée Fabert at Metz, formerly the Collège Royal, attended 1817 to 1823

stops.name: Paris, the law degree taken without love
stops.date_confidence: year attested (fr.wikipedia); month not established, defaulted to January
stops.campa: He returns to Paris for the law and takes his licence in 1826. The law is the family road: a Norman house that kept its lands wants a son in the magistracy, and the magistracy is one of the few careers a legitimist family can enter without swearing to much of anything. Tocqueville reads the code without love. The question he keeps returning to is one the code does not answer: why the order his parents nearly died for came apart, and whether what replaced it can be lived in by people who did not choose it.
suggested_refs: The Paris faculty of law under the Restoration, where he took his licence in 1826

stops.name: Versailles, the apprentice magistrate and Gustave de Beaumont
stops.date_confidence: year attested (fr.wikipedia); month of appointment not established
stops.campa: He is appointed juge auditeur at the tribunal of Versailles, an apprentice magistrate who is paid nothing and pleads badly; his voice is thin and he knows it. At the same tribunal he meets Gustave de Beaumont, older by three years, a better speaker and a steadier man, and the friendship made over case files lasts to his deathbed. In the winters that follow the two of them go into Paris to hear François Guizot lecture on the history of European civilization, where the fall of aristocracy is presented not as a crime but as a law.
suggested_refs: Guizot's Sorbonne lectures on the history of civilization in Europe, 1828 to 1830

stops.name: Versailles, the oath to a king he does not believe in
stops.date_confidence: attested that he swore the oath in 1830 (fr.wikipedia); the day is not established, defaulted to August
stops.campa: Charles X is driven out in three July days, and the marqués de Lafayette, seventy-two years old, presents the Duke of Orléans to the crowd from the balcony of the Hôtel de Ville wrapped in a tricolor flag. The Bourbons the Tocquevilles served are finished. Alexis swears loyalty to Louis-Philippe to keep his post at Versailles and is ashamed of it; his family reads the oath as apostasy and does not hide the reading. Within months he and Beaumont are drafting a proposal to leave France on public business.
suggested_refs: Lafayette on the balcony of the Hôtel de Ville, 31 July 1830, in contemporary prints

stops.name: Le Havre, the packet Havre puts to sea
stops.date_confidence: attested (fr.wikipedia: embarquement, 2 avril 1831)
stops.campa: The commission comes through: the two magistrates are to study the penitentiary systems of the United States and report on their application to France. They pay their own passage, and both of them know the prisons are a passport. On the second of April they board the packet Havre at the mouth of the Seine, twenty-five and twenty-eight years old, carrying letters of introduction and a list of questions about a country neither has seen. The crossing takes thirty-eight days of open water.
stops.quote: I confess that in America I saw more than America; I sought the image of democracy itself, with its inclinations, its character, its prejudices, and its passions, in order to learn what we have to fear or to hope from its progress.
stops.quote_source: Democracy in America, vol. 1, Author's Introduction, trans. Henry Reeve rev. Francis Bowen, Project Gutenberg ebook #815
suggested_refs: The transatlantic packet Havre, which carried them out in 1831 and home in 1832

stops.name: Newport, the first sight of the United States
stops.date_confidence: attested in aggregated secondary chronologies of the crossing; not confirmed against a ship's log in this research
stops.campa: After thirty-eight days the Havre makes Newport, and the two Frenchmen see the United States for the first time: a harbor of white wooden houses, no fortress above it, no livery in the street, nobody on the quay who looks either grand or wretched. There is no rank visible from the water. Tocqueville has crossed an ocean to inspect prisons and the first thing he writes down is about the absence of beggars. The observation goes, four years later, into the opening sentence of a book he does not yet know he is going to write.
stops.quote: Amongst the novel objects that attracted my attention during my stay in the United States, nothing struck me more forcibly than the general equality of conditions.
stops.quote_source: Democracy in America, vol. 1, Author's Introduction, trans. Henry Reeve rev. Francis Bowen, Project Gutenberg ebook #815
suggested_refs: Newport harbor in 1831, landfall of the packet Havre
sources: Aggregated secondary chronology of the 1831 crossing

stops.name: New York, coming ashore at the Battery
stops.date_confidence: attested (standard biographical accounts deriving from Pierson)
stops.campa: They land at the Battery and take lodgings, and the city adopts them inside a week: dinners with judges and bankers, invitations they cannot refuse, questions prepared in French and asked in an English Tocqueville is still learning. Seven years earlier the same water stairs received the marqués de Lafayette, the last living general of the American Revolution, under arches and cannon and a crowd of thousands. The two magistrates come ashore unnoticed, with no arch and no cannon, and it suits them; nothing has been staged for their benefit.
suggested_refs: Castle Garden and the Battery, landing place of Lafayette in 1824 and of Tocqueville in 1831
sources: Standard biographical accounts of the journey (Pierson)

stops.name: Ossining, the silent system at Sing Sing
stops.date_confidence: attested in aggregated chronology of the penitentiary tour; primary confirmation not retrieved
stops.campa: At Sing Sing they see the official object of the journey: hundreds of convicts quarrying stone under a rule of absolute silence, watched by a few dozen keepers who hold them by nothing except the certainty that the whole society outside the wall agrees with the wall. Tocqueville interviews prisoners one at a time in their cells and improves his English on them. The discipline impresses him and it frightens him. He is looking at a despotism built inside a republic, run at a profit, and barely noticed by the republic that pays for it.
suggested_refs: Sing Sing prison at Ossining under the silent congregate regime, 1831

stops.name: Auburn, the system that carries the town's name
stops.date_confidence: attested as a stop on the penitentiary tour; month approximate, day not established
stops.campa: At Auburn they study the model that will go into the report under the town's name: labor in common through the day, solitary cells through the night, silence enforced by the whip. It is the cheaper of the two American systems and the one they will recommend to France, with reservations they take care to print. The prison notebooks fill steadily, warden by warden. Beside them a second set fills faster, on juries, townships, newspapers, and the American habit of meeting in a room to do what a French prefect would do for them.
suggested_refs: Auburn State Prison, New York, model of congregate labor and nightly separation
sources: Standard biographical chronology of the penitentiary tour

stops.name: Detroit, buying horses for the woods
stops.date_confidence: attested as early to mid July 1831; the day is not established. Buffalo, their embarkation onto the lake steamers, is attested for the same weeks and is folded into this stop
stops.campa: From Buffalo they take a lake steamer west to Detroit, a fur and garrison town at the edge of the surveyed country. When they ask where a man can still find forest nobody has cut and Indians living as they lived, the land agents assume the Frenchmen want acreage and cannot be made to understand otherwise; nobody here travels toward wilderness, only through it. They buy horses, a compass, and provisions, and ride north into Michigan territory on a track that gives out inside a day's ride.
suggested_refs: Detroit in 1831, last town before the Michigan wilderness

stops.name: Saginaw, the far end of the wilderness ride
stops.date_confidence: attested from Tocqueville's own essay Quinze jours dans le désert; the exact days are not established
stops.campa: Saginaw is a handful of log houses at the end of the trail, with French half-breeds, Chippewa camps, and Americans who have come to buy the ground under both. It is the deepest he ever goes into country no surveyor has reached. Tocqueville sleeps in a bark lodge, hears wolves, and writes afterward that the pines will fall, that the tribes are dying by treaty and whiskey rather than by massacre, and that within one generation nothing here will be strange to anyone. He calls the essay Quinze jours dans le désert and does not publish it while he lives.
suggested_refs: Quinze jours dans le désert, the Saginaw essay, unpublished in his lifetime
sources: Tocqueville, Quinze jours dans le désert

stops.name: Niagara Falls, the cataract and the staircases
stops.date_confidence: attested in aggregated chronology of the journey (19 August 1831)
stops.campa: Coming back from Michigan they stop at Niagara. Tocqueville goes down under the sheet of falling water and comes up shaken, and then looks at the brink and sees the hotels going up, the guides, the hucksters, the paid staircases. He writes to a friend in France to hurry across the ocean if he wants to see this before it is spoiled, because within ten years the Americans will have put a mill at the foot of it. He is six weeks out of Saginaw, where there were no stairs, no guides, and nothing to pay.
suggested_refs: Niagara Falls in 1831, already under construction as a resort

stops.name: Montreal, the wreck of France on the other shore
stops.date_confidence: attested in aggregated chronology (23 August 1831); the Canadian leg runs roughly 20 August to 2 September, not July as one gathering source had it
stops.campa: In Montreal he hears his own language spoken in the street by farmers whose ancestors left Normandy before Louis XV lost them at a table in Paris. The signs above the shops are English, the courts are English, the money is English, and the people are French and Catholic and poor. Tocqueville, whose family is Norman, walks through a city that is roughly what his own country would be had it been conquered and left alive, and writes home that he has found the wreck of France on the far side of the ocean.
suggested_refs: Montreal under British rule in 1831, a French Catholic city with English courts

stops.name: Quebec, the old regime still standing
stops.date_confidence: attested as late August 1831 (en.wikipedia: a side trip to Montreal and Quebec City); the day is not established
stops.campa: He goes on to Quebec, the fortress capital on its rock, and finds the old regime intact where the Revolution never reached: seigneuries, tithes, parish priests with an authority no French curé has held in forty years, farmers content and incurious. In the courthouse he watches English judges hear French litigants through interpreters. The colony was cut off from France in 1763 and kept growing along the old lines. The language and the church have held here; the courts, the commerce, and the government of the place have not.
suggested_refs: The courts of Quebec in 1831, English judges and French litigants

stops.name: Boston, the township and the doctrine
stops.date_confidence: attested in aggregated chronology of the journey (arrival 9 September 1831)
stops.campa: Boston receives him better than any other American city: dinners with the legal and political men of the Commonwealth, whose institutions run back without a break to the Puritan town meeting. He fills a notebook here on the town meeting. Liberty in America is not kept in the federal constitution; it is kept in the township, in men who assemble to lay out a road, hire a schoolmaster, and tax themselves for both, and who therefore cannot be administered like children. He has been looking for the mechanism since Guizot's lecture room.
stops.quote: A new science of politics is indispensable to a new world. This, however, is what we think of least; launched in the middle of a rapid stream, we obstinately fix our eyes on the ruins which may still be described upon the shore we have left, whilst the current sweeps us along, and drives us backwards towards the gulf.
stops.quote_source: Democracy in America, vol. 1, Author's Introduction (mid-Introduction), trans. Henry Reeve rev. Francis Bowen, Project Gutenberg ebook #815
suggested_refs: New England town meeting records, the institution he made the hinge of the book

stops.name: Philadelphia, the solitary cells of Cherry Hill
stops.date_confidence: attested in aggregated chronology (interviews at Cherry Hill, 12 October 1831)
stops.campa: At Cherry Hill they meet the rival system: each convict alone in a vaulted cell under a skylight, without the sight or the sound of another man for years together. The two Frenchmen interview them one at a time, and the answers unsettle them; the solitude straightens some and empties others. This is Benjamin Franklin's city, where the Quakers who invented the penitentiary meant it as mercy put in the place of the gallows. They leave with the material of their report and with the two systems set against each other, the silent and the separate, for a ministry in Paris to choose between.
suggested_refs: Eastern State Penitentiary at Cherry Hill, the separate system, opened 1829

stops.name: Baltimore, an hour with the last signer
stops.date_confidence: attested in secondary accounts of the journey; the day is not established. Carroll was 94, not 95 as some accounts give
stops.campa: In Baltimore he is taken up by the old Catholic gentry of Maryland, the nearest thing the United States keeps to an aristocracy, and brought to see Charles Carroll of Carrollton, ninety-four years old, the last man alive who signed the Declaration of Independence. George Washington has been dead thirty-two years by then and Thomas Jefferson five. The founding is one old man away from passing out of living memory, and a French visitor of twenty-six sits with him and takes notes for a book about what the founders' country has since become.
suggested_refs: Charles Carroll of Carrollton in his ninety-fifth year, last surviving signer

stops.name: Pittsburgh, boarding the Fourth of July
stops.date_confidence: attested as the second half of November 1831; the day is not established. One gathering source placed the whole descent in December, which cannot be reconciled with four days at Cincinnati in early December
stops.campa: At the forks of the Ohio they board the steamboat Fourth of July and start down the river. Their leave still has months to run and the plan has grown well past prisons: they mean to see the slave states, the Mississippi, and New Orleans before turning for home. It is late November and the water is low. Ahead of them lie a wreck, a river frozen solid, three weeks of overland stages through Tennessee and Kentucky, and the one scene that will open his chapter on the three races of the continent.
suggested_refs: The Point at Pittsburgh, head of Ohio River steamboat navigation in 1831
sources: Standard chronology of the southward leg

segments.name: Down the Rivers, into the Winter

stops.name: Wheeling, the Fourth of July on the Burlington Bar
stops.date_confidence: attested as late November 1831; the day is not established. The gathering pass dated the wreck to December, corrected against the Cincinnati stay
stops.campa: Below Wheeling, in Virginia water, the Fourth of July strikes the Burlington Bar and stops there with a hole in her. The passengers are put ashore on the bank to wait for whatever comes down next. It is the first of the accidents that turn the southern leg from a river passage into an ordeal: low water, then ice, then a stagecoach over roads that are felled trees in mud. Tocqueville, who has been coughing since Michigan, works through all of it and writes at night in taverns full of men who spit and talk politics.
suggested_refs: The Burlington Bar on the Ohio near Wheeling, where the Fourth of July struck rock
sources: New York Times historical account of the 1831 journey

stops.name: Cincinnati, the two banks of one river
stops.date_confidence: attested: four days at Cincinnati in December 1831. The gathering pass had this stop as a reconstruction; it is attested
stops.campa: Four days at Cincinnati, a town that was forest thirty years ago and now has warehouses, foundries, and no ruins at all. Tocqueville stands on the free bank and looks across at Kentucky, and the two shores hand him the cleanest experiment in America: the same river, the same soil, the same climate, and on one side men who work for themselves and on the other men who own men and let the ground go slack. He writes it up as an argument about slavery in which he never has to raise his voice, because the geography argues for him.
suggested_refs: The Cincinnati public landing, 1831, free bank facing slaveholding Kentucky

stops.name: Memphis, the Choctaw cross the frozen river
stops.date_confidence: attested that they were stranded eight days at Memphis in December 1831; the day of the Choctaw crossing is not fixed in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Stranded eight days at Memphis waiting for a boat, he watches a column of Choctaw come down to the water in the hardest cold of the year: old men, women carrying newborns, the sick, moving west under the treaty signed at Dancing Rabbit Creek the year before, which was made possible by the Removal Act President Andrew Jackson signed at the Capitol in May 1830. They cross among the ice. The dogs, left on the eastern bank, understand at the last moment and throw themselves into the river after their people. He sets the scene at the head of his chapter on the three races.
suggested_refs: Choctaw removal parties crossing the Mississippi at Memphis, winter of 1831
sources: Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1, ch. 18
Aggregated account of the Memphis stopover

stops.name: The Mississippi south of Memphis, a big man in Cherokee dress
stops.date_confidence: attested: Houston boarded a New Orleans steamboat with a Cherokee delegation two days after Christmas 1831 and the conversation is in Tocqueville's notebooks. The traditional version placing the meeting in a Memphis hotel is not supported
stops.campa: A boat finally comes down and takes them south. Aboard, a big man in Cherokee dress joins them with a delegation of Cherokee: Sam Houston, former governor of Tennessee, who walked out of the office and the state to live with the tribe and has not yet gone to Texas. Tocqueville questions him for hours on the Indian nations, the whiskey trade, and the western land, and copies the answers into his notebook. This is the same reach of river where a Missouri boy will learn the pilot's trade a generation later and take his name, Mark Twain, off the leadsman's cry.
suggested_refs: Tocqueville's notebook record of the conversation with Sam Houston, December 1831
sources: HistoryNet, The Day Sam Houston Met Alexis de Tocqueville

stops.name: New Orleans, three days at the far end
stops.date_confidence: attested: arrival and a three-day stay around 1 January 1832
stops.campa: Three days in New Orleans, the far end of the journey: a French city under American law, Catholic, Creole, and built on the sale of people. He hears his own language in the market and in the courtroom, and he sees an auction. The two Americas he has been sorting since Boston stand on one street here, the free port and the block. Seventeen of the twenty-four states are behind him and some seven thousand miles, and he turns north with a division in the union that the constitution he has been studying does not mention.
suggested_refs: The French Quarter levee at New Orleans, southernmost point of the American journey

stops.name: Washington, a glass of Madeira with President Jackson
stops.date_confidence: attested: received on the afternoon of 19 January 1832 (Journal of the Early Republic, Tocqueville and the American Presidency). The gathering pass invented a second, earlier Washington visit in October 1831; there was one visit
stops.campa: On the afternoon of the nineteenth of January they are received at the President's house by Andrew Jackson, who offers them a glass of Madeira and not much else. There is no guard at the door. Tocqueville is unimpressed and says so in his notes, setting down a man of violent temper and middling gifts raised up by a party rather than chosen by the country. Six months later Jackson vetoes the Bank of the United States and takes the quarrel straight to the voters, which is the executive Tocqueville has just described before it has finished happening.
suggested_refs: The President's House in January 1832, unguarded and open to callers
sources: Journal of the Early Republic, Tocqueville and the American Presidency

stops.name: Philadelphia, the last overland stage
stops.date_confidence: date attested; direction disputed. The source reads that before dawn on 3 February 1832 they took a stagecoach to Philadelphia, then to New York, which is read here as departure from Washington and arrival at Philadelphia. The gathering pass read it as departure from Philadelphia
stops.campa: Before dawn on the third of February they take the stage north out of Washington and reach Philadelphia, the city where George Washington governed from a rented house on Market Street when the republic was three years old. The prison report is written already in their heads. The other book is in the trunk in a few hundred pages of notes taken in taverns, courtrooms, cells, forests, and steamboats. Nine months and most of the money are gone, and the Ministry in Paris has been asking for some time when its magistrates mean to come home.
suggested_refs: The President's House on Market Street, Philadelphia, seat of the executive 1790 to 1800

stops.name: New York, the Havre stands out to sea
stops.date_confidence: attested (fr.wikipedia: rembarquement de New York le 20 février 1832)
stops.campa: On the twentieth of February they board the Havre, the ship that carried them out, and stand off the Battery where they came ashore nine months before. Behind them are seventeen states, Lower Canada, some seven thousand miles, and a mission on penitentiaries carried out in full and in writing. In the baggage is the material of an entirely different book. Tocqueville is twenty-six and will never cross the Atlantic again; everything he says about America for the rest of his life comes out of these notebooks.
suggested_refs: The American notebooks of 1831-32, source of everything he later wrote on the United States

stops.name: Paris, the report the government paid for
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia, Gustave de Beaumont); month not established
stops.campa: The debt is discharged first. Tocqueville and Beaumont publish Du système pénitentiaire aux États-Unis, et de son application en France, the report they were sent to write, weighing Auburn against Cherry Hill, costing both, and recommending a French version of the cheaper one. It is a serious book by two men who spent the better part of a year interviewing convicts through cell gratings. It is also the receipt for the passport. With it paid, Tocqueville shuts himself up with the other notebooks and begins.
suggested_refs: Du système pénitentiaire aux États-Unis, Paris 1833, the official mission report

stops.name: Versailles, Mary Mottley
stops.date_confidence: attested as 1833 (en.wikipedia: met at Versailles in 1833, married in 1836); month not established. One gathering source dated the meeting to 1835, which does not fit the 1836 marriage
stops.campa: He meets Mary Mottley at Versailles: English, Protestant, without family or fortune, some years older than he is. His own family calls the attachment a disaster and keeps calling it that for three years. The same year he crosses to England for five weeks and looks hard at an aristocracy still standing, the thing his own class has stopped being, and starts the comparison that runs underneath everything he writes afterward about equality. He marries her in 1836 and stays married twenty-three years. There are no children.
suggested_refs: Mary Mottley, later Marie de Tocqueville, in contemporary portraits

stops.name: Paris, De la démocratie en Amérique, volume one
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia, Democracy in America); month not established
stops.campa: The first volume appears in Paris and makes him famous inside a month. Royalists and republicans both claim it, which tells him he wrote what he intended: not a defense of democracy and not an indictment, but a description of a change he holds to be providential and irreversible, with a full inventory of what it costs. He is twenty-nine. A decade later an exiled Argentine schoolmaster, Domingo Faustino Sarmiento, writes Facundo on the method of this book, then sails to the United States to check the method against the country.
stops.quote: The equality of conditions is the fundamental fact from which all others seem to be derived, and the central point at which all my observations constantly terminated.
stops.quote_source: Democracy in America, vol. 1, Author's Introduction, trans. Henry Reeve rev. Francis Bowen, Project Gutenberg ebook #815
suggested_refs: The first Paris edition of De la démocratie en Amérique, Gosselin, 1835

stops.name: Dublin, an aristocracy with no duties
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia); months not established, defaulted to July
stops.campa: He returns to England and goes on with Beaumont to Ireland, where the two of them find an aristocracy holding every privilege and owing no obligation, ruling a Catholic peasantry already at the edge of starvation ten years before the potato fails. Tocqueville, an aristocrat who has spent five years arguing that his own class fell because it stopped being useful, walks into cabins with no windows and no floor. Beaumont turns the journey into a book, L'Irlande sociale, politique et religieuse, published in 1839.
suggested_refs: Beaumont, L'Irlande sociale, politique et religieuse (1839), from this journey

stops.name: Paris, the marriage his family opposed
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia, fr.wikipedia); the month and the place of the ceremony are not established in sources consulted, and are a stated gap
stops.campa: He marries Mary Mottley against his family, and the marriage holds for twenty-three years, to his death. They have no children. She reads his drafts, keeps his correspondence, and at the end nurses him through the disease of the lungs that kills him. That autumn the couple travel by Metz and Strasbourg to Basel and Bern, and he studies the Swiss cantons the way he studied New England townships, looking for self-government at the smallest scale at which it can be found working.
suggested_refs: The Swiss journey of September 1836, Metz to Strasbourg to Basel and Bern

stops.name: Valognes, the Manche sends him to the Chamber
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia, fr.wikipedia); the polling day is not established, defaulted to January
stops.campa: The Manche sends him to the Chamber of Deputies for Valognes, the district his family has held land in since long before the Revolution. He keeps the seat until the Republic replaces the Chamber in 1848. He is a poor speaker in an assembly that rewards nothing else, thin-voiced and better on paper, and he never gathers a following; the deputies hear him out the way one hears a witness rather than a leader. He votes with no party reliably and writes the reports nobody else wants, on prisons and on Algeria.
suggested_refs: The Valognes constituency of the Manche, his seat from 1839 to 1848

stops.name: Paris, the second volume and the softer despotism
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia, Democracy in America); month not established
stops.campa: The second volume appears five years after the first and sells worse. It is colder, more abstract, and about something the first volume only glanced at: what equality does to the inside of a man. Democratic peoples, he writes, are not crushed by a tyrant; they are pressed on by each other until each holds the opinion all hold and takes it for his own. The tutelary power he sketches at the end, mild, provident, absolute, keeping grown citizens in perpetual childhood, is not a memory of America. It is a forecast.
stops.quote: For myself, when I feel the hand of power lie heavy on my brow, I care but little to know who oppresses me; and I am not the more disposed to pass beneath the yoke, because it is held out to me by the arms of a million of men.
stops.quote_source: Democracy in America, vol. 2, part I, ch. II, trans. Henry Reeve, Project Gutenberg ebook #816
suggested_refs: Democracy in America, volume II, Paris 1840

stops.name: Algiers, the Académie and the war of conquest
stops.date_confidence: both the Académie election and the first Algerian visit are attested for 1841; months not established
stops.campa: The year the Académie française elects him at thirty-six, he crosses to Algiers for the first time and rides into a war of conquest eleven years old. The emir Abdelkader holds two thirds of the country from a capital that moves on camels, and Marshal Bugeaud is answering him by burning the crops of whole tribes. Tocqueville comes home and writes that France must keep Algeria, that the razzia is regrettable and necessary, and that a European power which withdraws is finished. The man who measured the tyranny of the majority at Boston recommends the destruction of an Arab state.
suggested_refs: Bugeaud's razzia campaigns against the Emirate, seen at first hand in 1841

stops.name: Algiers, the second crossing and the Travail sur l'Algérie
stops.date_confidence: second visit attested as 1846, the Travail sur l'Algérie as 1847; months not established
stops.campa: He crosses again in 1846 and comes back with a harder report. The Travail sur l'Algérie of 1847 tells the Chamber that the army governs by expedient, that the Arabs have been left poorer and more ignorant than France found them, and that domination must nevertheless be permanent. Nine years earlier he had written letters hoping for marriage between French and Arabs and one people made out of both. The same season he tries to build a Young Left around labour reform, and the ground goes out from under the whole Chamber before either project can matter.
suggested_refs: Travail sur l'Algérie, 1847, his report to the Chamber of Deputies

stops.name: Paris, the twenty-fourth of February
stops.date_confidence: attested, from his own account in the Souvenirs
stops.campa: The monarchy he swore to in 1830 falls in a morning. Tocqueville comes down his own staircase, meets the cook returning from the street with a story he cannot follow about the government massacring the poor, and walks out into a quarter with the shops shut and nothing moving in the road. He has spent thirteen years explaining that the democratic revolution cannot be reversed and that France keeps trying to stop it with regimes. He watches this one end from the pavement, and sets the morning down from memory two years later.
stops.quote: On leaving my bed-room, I met the cook, who had been out; the good woman was quite beside herself, and poured out a sorrowing rigmarole, of which I failed to understand a word, except that the Government was massacring the poor people. I went downstairs at once, and had no sooner set foot in the street than I breathed for the first time the atmosphere of revolution.
stops.quote_source: Recollections (Souvenirs), account of 24 February 1848, English translation, archive.org recollectionsofa00tocquoft
suggested_refs: The Souvenirs, written 1850-1851, published posthumously 1893

stops.name: Paris, the Constituent Assembly and the June Days
stops.date_confidence: attested: elected 23 April 1848 by the Manche. The gathering pass gave 25 April, corrected against the French text
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of April the Manche sends him to the Constituent Assembly of the Second Republic, and he is put on the commission that drafts the constitution, where he argues against a president elected by the whole nation and loses the argument. In June the workers of Paris rise against the closing of the national workshops, and the Assembly hands the city to General Cavaignac. Tocqueville votes for that and walks the barricaded streets while it is carried out. He calls the four days afterward a war of class against class and does not pretend he stood outside it.
suggested_refs: The constitutional commission of the Second Republic, and the June Days of 1848

stops.name: Paris, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
stops.date_confidence: attested as June 1849; the day of taking office is not established in sources consulted
stops.campa: He becomes Minister of Foreign Affairs in Odilon Barrot's government, serving a President of the Republic named Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, elected by universal male suffrage over every candidate the Assembly preferred. Tocqueville had argued in committee that this manner of election would produce exactly this man. He holds the ministry a matter of months and works it while coughing blood. The constitution he helped draft is now being administered by one of its authors on behalf of an executive already counting the days to the end of his term.
suggested_refs: The Barrot ministry of 1849, in which he held the Quai d'Orsay

stops.name: Saint-Lô, president of the council of the Manche
stops.date_confidence: attested: elected 6 August 1849 on the second ballot, 24 votes of 44. The gathering pass gave 27 August, corrected against the French record
stops.campa: On the sixth of August the general council of the Manche elects him its president on the second ballot, twenty-four votes out of forty-four, and he keeps the chair until 1852. National office comes and goes in months; the department is the piece of French public life he actually holds, roads and hospitals and drainage in the country his family has farmed since before the Terror. It is the nearest thing France offers him to the New England township he spent a book admiring, and he keeps it after everything else is taken.
suggested_refs: The conseil général de la Manche, which he presided over from 1849 to 1852

stops.name: Vincennes, arrested by the thing he described
stops.date_confidence: attested: the coup of 2 December 1851 and his brief detention; the exact hours of the detention are not established
stops.campa: On the second of December Louis-Napoléon dissolves the Assembly with the army. Tocqueville joins the deputies who gather to declare the President deposed, and the whole meeting is arrested and marched out to the fortress of Vincennes, where he is held with his colleagues and released after a short confinement. He is forty-six and his political life is over. The empire that follows is the outcome he sketched in the abstract in 1840, a mild absolute power resting on the votes of men who prefer quiet, and it has now had him in a cell.
suggested_refs: The donjon of Vincennes, holding place of the deputies arrested on 2 December 1851

stops.name: Tocqueville, the château and the archives
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month not established. Coordinates are those of the village and château, 49.67 N 1.34 W; one lens of the research pool placed the château at 49.6167 / -1.4, about seven kilometres off in open country
stops.campa: He withdraws to the château at Tocqueville in the Cotentin, the house his family took its name from, and turns from politics to paper. The plan is a book on Napoleon. What he finds underneath is the Revolution, and underneath the Revolution the monarchy that made it. He reads intendants' correspondence and cahiers de doléances in provincial depots for years, working the way he worked in American prisons, one file and one interview at a time, and living most of the year in the country his ancestors administered.
stops.quote: Removed for a time from the scene of public life, I am constrained, in the midst of my solitude, to turn my thoughts upon myself, or rather to reflect upon contemporary events in which I have taken part or acted as a witness.
stops.quote_source: Recollections (Souvenirs), opening sentence, written 1850-1851, published 1893; English translation, archive.org recollectionsofa00tocquoft
suggested_refs: The Château de Tocqueville, Manche, where the Ancien Régime was written

stops.name: Paris, L'Ancien Régime et la Révolution
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia); month not established
stops.campa: L'Ancien Régime et la Révolution appears and argues the thing nobody in France wanted argued: that the Revolution did not break the old monarchy's work but finished it, that centralization, the ruin of local liberties, and the leveling of ranks were all under way well before 1789, and that the men of 1789 inherited the machine they believed they had built. The second volume, on the Revolution itself, is planned and never written. He is coughing steadily now, and the archives have taken the strength he had left.
suggested_refs: L'Ancien Régime et la Révolution, Paris 1856, volume I; the second volume never completed
sources: en.wikipedia, L'Ancien Régime et la Révolution

stops.name: Cannes, the lungs give out at fifty-three
stops.date_confidence: attested (en.wikipedia, fr.wikipedia)
stops.campa: They send him south for the winter air. He dies at Cannes on the sixteenth of April, fifty-three years old, of the tuberculosis that had been working on him since the American rivers. Gustave de Beaumont is at the bedside, thirty-two years after the two of them met over case files at the tribunal of Versailles and went off together to look at American prisons. Mary Mottley survives him. Beaumont takes the papers in hand and begins editing the collected works and letters, a labour left unfinished at his own death and completed by his widow.
suggested_refs: Beaumont's edition of the Oeuvres complètes, begun 1859, finished by his widow

stops.name: Tocqueville, the grave in the village cemetery
stops.date_confidence: burial in the village cemetery of Tocqueville is attested; the day is not established in sources consulted and is reconstructed here as shortly after the death. The tomb inscription could not be confirmed and is a stated gap
stops.campa: He is buried in the cemetery of the village that carries the family name, a few hundred metres from the house where he wrote his last book. In France the reputation goes under for most of a century, uncongenial to republicans and socialists alike, and is raised again after 1945 by Raymond Aron and François Furet. In America it never sinks. The country he described at twenty-six quotes him constantly and puts in his mouth a sentence he never wrote, that America is great because she is good. The words are twentieth-century pulpit oratory. The book that made them sound like his is not.
suggested_refs: The Tocqueville family plot in the village cemetery, Manche
